articles.title: What Jensen Huang's return teaches China's Xi about Trump
articles.summary: Huang being back at the helm of Nvidia is no guarantee of relief for Beijing.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
A comeback for the ages: Trump's influence on Huang's return to Nvidia By Laura Bicker China correspondent 
- Published 24 November 2026 
Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO has riveted the world - including China, where it has become the top trending post on Weibo, the country's biggest social media platform. 
Most users are pleased to see the return of the influential billionaire, who declared that he loved China, before videos appeared online of him eating noodles and drinking milk tea during a visit in May. Some wondered why - in the video of him returning to Nvidia's headquarters - he is not wearing one of his leather jackets. 
But to many, Huang's return, which is being dubbed one of the greatest U-turns of all time, seems like a vindication for China. 
That's probably how Xi Jinping sees it too. 
Beijing has dismissed claims that one of the women who had an affair with Jensen Huang had been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security, its version of the CIA, as a spy. Chinese state media has also framed the spy saga as a smear campaign orchestrated by China hawks in Washington. The Global Times, a Communist Party mouthpiece, described it as a "witch hunt". 
Now the White House, and President Donald Trump himself, have said Huang poses no national security threat, although investigations into the spy allegations are still ongoing. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Trunmp and Xi ahead of their meeting in Shenzhen last week 
Xi will have learned many lessons from this scandal, especially about Trump's pressure points. 
For one, the fact that Huang's reappointment came so soon after Xi's meetings last week with Trump in Shenzhen could be read as a sign that direct engagement is an effective way to influence Washington. 
Trump has said the two men discussed Huang, but did not elaborate further. Beijing has not commented. 
The episode has also reinforced the view among Chinese officials that there are two camps in Washington: those in favour of restricting Chinese access to cutting edge tech to protect US national security, and those, like Huang, who believe that such restrictions will not limit Beijing's ambitions. 
Huang has repeatedly argued that US export controls will force Chinese firms like Huawei to build independent alternatives - all the while shutting American companies out of the world's second-largest economy. 
But him being back at the helm of Nvidia is no guarantee of relief for Beijing. 
Rather, the sale of advanced chips will remain a key point of contention between the US and China, especially as the two sides try to reach a trade deal before another Trump-Xi meeting, which is expected in December. 
Already new rules are being put in place that will worry Beijing. 
The US Bureau of Industry and Security is tightening restrictions by targeting not only the direct export of advanced chips to China, but also Chinese firms' ability to use computing power in data centres overseas. 
The measures are designed to close potential loopholes that allow Chinese companies to access advanced Nvidia and AMD chips through cloud providers operating in third countries, including Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand. 
China has yet to react with measures of its own. But investors will be watching closely for any escalation which could weigh on US equity markets. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Jensen Huang at an Nvidia event in Berlin in October 
And having seen how eager Trump is to keep things stable, Xi may see this as leverage. 
He now knows Trump is so worried about the stock market that he is prepared to intervene in the HR decisions of the world's biggest company. The president has also personally invested in Nvidia, although the White House has emphasised that Trump has placed his businesses in a trust managed by his sons. 
China has already used its considerable chokehold over the world's rare earth metals to bring the US to the negotiating table over trade. 
If Washington restricts chip exports and Beijing retaliates, that could be the start of a cycle that has a profound effect on the stock market because American companies, from car makers to defence firms to chip manufacturers, all rely on rare earths. 
What China has realised is that more trouble lies ahead as it tries to build what it describes as a "constructive strategic relationship" with the US. 
Trump's tariffs are no longer at the heart of that tussle. Now it's about control of critical technology and minerals which could, in turn, affect each side's military influence and economic power. 
What happens next will depend on how the Jensen Huang saga unfolds because it is far from over. 
Huang is set to testify before Congress next month, and come January, a Democrat-controlled Congress will raise the pressure. Even some Republican lawmakers have made clear they want answers. 
Arkansas senator Tom Cotton wrote on X that the Nvidia controversy "is just the tip of the iceberg and it's not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back".

articles.title: Huawei found guilty of stealing trade secrets but acquitted of racketeering
articles.summary: The verdict follows a months-long trial in New York.
articles.full_text:
Image source, REUTERS/Jane Rosenberg Image caption, 
Defence lawyer Brian Heberlig makes closing arguments at the Huawei Technologies trial at Brooklyn federal court on November 17. By Rachel Clun Business reporter 
- Published 24 November 2026 Updated 1 hour ago 
Huawei has been found guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud, but not guilty of the more serious overarching racketeering charge in a landmark case in the US. 
In a two-month trial, prosecutors accused the Chinese technology and telecommunications giant of lying, cheating and stealing to gain any competitive advantage. 
Huawei's defence team argued that prosecutors had decided Huawei was a criminal organisation and built its case from there, but the firm's success was due to its own innovation. 
Huawei said , external the racketeering acquittal "confirms that these allegations lack factual basis", adding that it would "take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests". 
Jurors in a Brooklyn court found Huawei guilty of 10 out of 12 counts, which included conspiracy to violate US sanctions. 
However, the jury declined to convict Huawei of the racketeering conspiracy charge, which required members to find the firm acted like a criminal enterprise. 
Federal prosecutors first announced the charges against Huawei in 2019, after the dramatic arrest in late 2018 of senior executive Meng Wanzhou in Canada. 
Meng, also known as Cathy Meng, was held for three years in Canada before she was released to return to China through a deal with US prosecutors. 
During closing arguments last week, assistant US attorney Meredith Arfa told jurors Huawei spent 20 years doing whatever it took to expand its business, including lying to banks about its business dealings in Iran and stealing technology secrets from rival firms to ensure it had a competitive edge. 
"For decades, Huawei and three of its subsidiaries conducted their business in the United States on the basis of lies and theft," US Attorney General Todd Blanche said in statement , external . 
"Thanks to the work of the FBI and our federal prosecutors, those who engaged in these criminal activities will be held accountable." 
However, defence attorney Brian Heberlig said it was by dint of hard work that Huawei's business had expanded with operations in 170 countries and more than 200,000 staff. 
Following the verdict, Heberlig told the BBC that Huawei was gratified that the jury had rejected the racketeering charge. 
"The RICO [Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act] count that alleged that Huawei was a corrupt organisation, with a corporate culture and policy of committing crime. That was, in our view, a significant overreach, and the jury soundly rejected it," he said. 
"Of course, we have mixed emotions about the rest of the verdict ... [we] thought that Huawei was deserving of acquittals across the board." 
Sentencing is planned for September 2027. Heberlig said there will be "significant advocacy" to achieve the lowest sentence possible. Following that, he said he fully expects Huawei to appeal. 
"If I know Huawei, that fight will continue, and the company's not going to rest until it's pursued every last argument it can through appeal, and hopefully, ultimately toward vindication," he said.

articles.title: These North Koreans say they were spied on, beaten and jailed for being Christian
articles.summary: A new report has testimonies from hundreds of defectors who say they were persecuted because of their faith.
articles.full_text:
Image source, KCNA via Getty Images Image caption, 
Kim Jong Un's communist regime is accused of brutal crackdowns on religious freedom in a new report By Jake Kwon Seoul correspondent 
- Published 5 hours ago 
Living in North Korea, Kim Bo-bin got used to praying with her eyes open. 
She found ingenious ways to keep her Christian faith a secret in the Communist dictatorship, which tightly controls how and where its citizens worship. Unauthorised displays of faith could land people in prison, she tells the BBC. 
So Kim would silently mouth hymns and clap with just two of her fingers. "In North Korea, if there are three people in a room, you are being spied on. So I would only close my eyes [and pray] when I lay on the floor." 
Now 44, Kim lives just outside the South Korean capital Seoul, where she fled 15 years ago. 
Her testimony - of how she prayed in secret for years, and was jailed and beaten for her faith - is part of a new report documenting the experiences of 570 North Korean escapees, most of whom say they experienced or witnessed anti-Christian persecution. 
Spanning five years and featuring interviews with defectors from across the country, the report by British human rights group Korea Future accuses Kim Jong Un's regime of repeatedly violating religious freedom through a system of surveillance, fear and violence. It suggests little has changed after sustained international pressure, with multiple incidents of suspected Christians being beaten and tortured as recently as last year. 
North Korea maintains that it allows religious freedom in spite of years of evidence heard by rights groups and the United Nations. While churches exist in Pyongyang, they are controlled by the state and widely seen as projecting an illusion of religious liberty. 
"The North Korean leader's authority is god-like," says Kang Dong-wan, professor at Dong-a University. "So they cannot allow gods whose authority is above him." Pyongyang fears that religious freedom may threaten the regime itself, he adds. 
Image source, Courtesy Kim Bo-bin Image caption, 
Kim Bo-bin has been living in South Korea for 15 years now 
First established in Korea in the late 1700s, Christianity exploded across the north after Protestant missionaries arrived in the 1880s. North Korea provides no figures on its Christian population but the UN has referred to estimates of 200,000 to 400,000 of them practising secretly, some of whom are detained in camps. 
Surveillance and control over religion, like many other aspects of North Korean life, intensified under Kim Jong Un, who succeeded his father in 2011. 
Three South Korean missionaries operating in the Chinese border region were arrested between 2013-2014 and sentenced to life in prison on charges of espionage and plotting a coup. It's not clear if they are still alive, as Seoul says Pyongyang has refused to share any information about the detainees. 
Pyongyang has also been cracking down on smuggled memory sticks containing South Korean-made videos of Christian sermons. In 2020, it passed a law - on Rejecting Reactionary Ideology and Culture - to block so-called "foreign influence". Owning Bibles and hosting services can now result in imprisonment, while distributing religious books or videos is punishable by death. 
Lessons against religion begin as early as kindergarten for most North Koreans. Children must attend "self-criticism" sessions at school in which they are warned against "superstitions", widely understood to refer to Christianity and other faiths. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
An image from 2010 showing the inside of a state-sanctioned church in Pyongyang 
This is what Kim Bo-bin recalls being taught. The faiths Koreans have long practised - Christianity since the 18th Century and shamanism, a millennia-old practice rooted in ancestral spirit worship - were dismissed as superstitions. 
Her teachers never mentioned that Kim Il Sung himself was born into a fervently Christian family, or that Pyongyang had once been dubbed the "Jerusalem of the East." 
Rather, every child and adult is expected to know North Korea's foundational Ten Principles by heart. They state that citizens must hold the "firm perspective" they know of "nothing greater than the great comrades" Kim Il Sung, the founder of North Korea, his son Kim Jong Il and the ruling party. The "smallest attempt" to dent this authority must not be tolerated, it adds. 
The report documents both the indoctrination as well as the constant surveillance, with police and a network of neighbourhood spies monitoring suspicious activities. A former police informant says she was instructed to gather information on neighbours' worshipping, and handed a memo by an officer describing Christianity as an "anti-socialist activity". 
North Korean authorities are also reported to hold intergenerational records of families' beliefs condemning Christians' children and grandchildren to a life without higher education or decent career prospects. 
All of this illustrates how various North Korean institutions, including schools and the police, control its citizens' beliefs from "cradle to the grave," co-author James Burt says. 
And yet many North Koreans turn to religion because their lives are so precarious, he adds. Faith offers them something that the state ideology "with its rigid doctrines and disconnect from their lived realities" cannot. 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
North Koreans pay tribute to statues of the late Kim Il Sung and Kim Jong Il 
Kim Bo-bin grew up in North Hamgyong province, along the border with China. It was a remote, impoverished part of the country where those deemed "untrustworthy" by the state ended up, such as landowners and Christians. 
Stuck at the bottom of a state-enforced hierarchy, this "hostile class" had little chance of moving up the ladder. Many of Kim's neighbours were barred from higher education and government positions, or ever living in Pyongyang. 
One of them was an exiled "crazy grandma" who used to disappear into a coal shed every morning to chant words 10-year-old Kim didn't recognise. "One day, [the grandma] told me we go from ashes to ashes and dust to dust," she recalls. It was only 12 years later, when she encountered a Bible for the first time in her life that she realised the grandma was a Christian. 
When a devastating famine began in the late 1990s, North Hamgyong was one of the first regions to starve because it was cut off from the state's food supply which prioritised Pyongyang. Millions were killed in what the regime described euphemistically as the "Arduous March". It was a time when many North Koreans crossed into China seeking food and work. 
Kim was one of them. Aged 22 in 2003, she took what she believed was a job opportunity in China offered by a friend's aunt. But once she crossed the border, she was forced into marriage with a Chinese man and became pregnant. 
While picking up a free pram for her newborn daughter at a building adorned with a cross, she encountered a missionary for the first time. Kim would join a growing group of people who discovered Christianity in China - a group that Pyongyang saw as a threat when they were returned to the North, according to Prof Kang. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
A view of the city of Chongjin in North Korea's North Hamgyong province 
Kim was arrested in China in 2007 and deported. During interrogation, she says North Korean secret police asked her if she'd ever worn a cross on her neck. She pretended not to understand. She told the police she only recognised the symbol from hospital buildings. 
Kim Bo-bin says it was God's blessing the interrogator seemed more interested in whether she intended to flee to South Korea, a grave offence. She says she was beaten for 23 days and sentenced to three years of hard labour at a prison. Her story tallies with multiple accounts in Korea Future's report of extreme police violence causing broken bones and severe bleeding. 
Lee Young-joo, who Kim Bo-bin met in prison also after being deported from China, tells the BBC she was interrogated about whether she'd met any missionaries, been to a church or seen a Bible. "Of course you must deny all of it. I said no, I haven't seen it," she told them. 
In her prison cell, Lee says she'd keep her eyes open, begging God to save her life. Whenever anyone shut their eyes, guards would swear and shout: "Are you praying?" 
Lee is glad she wasn't found to be a Christian, because she says she "would have been sent to a political prisoners' camp. I would be tortured and never allowed to leave and be buried there." This is a widely-held fear among defectors, although Korea Future's report did not hear any first-hand testimonies of Christians being held in such camps. 
Lee, who previously shared with the BBC the abuse she suffered inside prison, says she was sentenced to three-and-half years. Outside of hard labour, she would spend time praying, sometimes with other Christian inmates. They would hold hands and whisper Bible verses from memory. 
Image source, BBC/ Hosu Lee Image caption, 
Lee Young-joo first met a Christian after she escaped from North Korea into China 
She and Kim Bo-bin eventually returned home after serving their sentences, where they continued to practise their religion in secret, they tell the BBC. 
Kim says she managed to convert her younger sister and other relatives: "My aunt's walls are thick. The neighbours can't hear us so I quietly taught them hymns and about the all-knowing and all-powerful God." 
Lee tells the BBC her mother was horrified when she learned of her Christian faith. Undeterred, she told her that she would escape again to join her daughter, who had been left in China as Lee was arrested and deported. When her mother protested, she responded saying they could all live together later. 
Her incredulous mother asked: where? "In heaven," she replied. 
Today, Lee attends a small church of North Korean escapees in Seoul. She prays daily, to thank God for the chicken soup and the stroll along the river. She prays for her daughter, who escaped with her in 2010, to find a nice Christian man to marry. Her mother died in North Korea some years after her escape, she was told. 
Kim managed to flee to South Korea eventually, in 2012, at the age of 30, along with her daughter. She prays throughout the day - and not silently. At church on Sundays, she is the loudest singer.

articles.title: Solomon Islands ends controversial security pact with China for Australian treaty
articles.summary: Solomon Islands leader Matthew Wale said his country would no longer be a point of regional uncertainty.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Australia and the Solomon Islands have signed a new treaty on security and economics By Helen Davidson Reporting from Sydney 
- Published 1 hour ago 
The Solomon Islands has signed a "historic" treaty with Australia, after reportedly telling China it was ending a controversial security pact signed in 2022. 
At a press conference in Canberra on Wednesday, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Solomon Islands counterpart Matthew Wale said the new treaty would ensure that Australia was the Pacific nation's "security partner of choice". 
In 2022 the Solomon Islands, then under the leadership of now-Opposition Leader Manasseh Sogavare, signed a security and policing pact with Beijing . 
There were fears the pact gave China a crucial military and strategic foothold in the Pacific amid a battle for influence in the region with the US. 
On Tuesday, Australian media outlets reported that Honiara had told Beijing it would not renew the pact, understood to be expiring in April 2027. 
Wale told reporters on Wednesday there were "ongoing discussions" with China but he was "unable to talk about" the pact, because of a non-disclosure agreement. 
He said the treaty with Australia provided a reset after several years in which the Solomon Islands had been a point of "uncertainty and doubt in the region". 
"Those days are done, gone," Wale said. 
Albanese said the treaty would strengthen the two countries' security partnership. 
"Backing our Pacific neighbours is an investment in Australia's own security and our own prosperity." 
"We'll do that in a way that completely respects Solomon Islands sovereignty and its right to make its own decisions." 
On Tuesday China's foreign ministry spokesman, Guo Jiukan, did not confirm or deny that the pact had been terminated. 
"There is no element of geopolitical rivalry or bloc confrontation in cooperation between China and Pacific island countries, including the Solomon Islands," Guo said. 
The pact was never publicly released, but leaked excerpts revealed it gave China extensive involvement in security and policing including deploying its own officers to the Solomon Islands, and allowed it to establish a quasi military base. 
It was a "massive coup" for Beijing, said Lowy Institute Research Fellow, Dr Connor Graham, but its unprecedented scale sparked alarm in the Pacific and the West. 
Wednesday's treaty had delivered "an enormous win for Canberra", and "closes the loop" on a series of security deals Canberra signed with Pacific nations in the wake of the Solomons-China pact. 
"That [China pact] was the thing that put fear in the hearts of diplomats in Washington and Canberra," he told the BBC. 
William Yang, the International Crisis Group's Senior Analyst for North East Asia, said the end of China's "flagship" Pacific deal and the signing of the new treaty also reaffirmed the Pacific's "longstanding consensus-based decision-making model, especially in the security space". 
Under the new treaty, the Solomon Islands commits to prior consultation with Australia on critical infrastructure and to ensure any security cooperations are with Pacific Islands Forum members. China is a dialogue partner but not a member of the forum. 
Honiara also commits to its sensitive infrastructure remaining "free from militarisation, any form of foreign interference or unauthorised access", and to not permit its territory to be used for any foreign military or security base. 
The Solomons will receive support for its free education system and sports programs, improved visa arrangements, and support for the expansion of affordable and renewable energy and infrastructure development. 
Earlier this week the ABC reported the package promised more than A$980m (£460.7m, $648,000) in additional funding, citing leaked text messages. The BBC has not independently verified the text messages. 
Wale visited Australia to sign the treaty, accompanied by two dozen Solomons MPs. He and Albanese said the size of the delegation demonstrated that the treaty had strong support from the country's parliament, after years of political instability - largely driven by disagreement over the country's relationship with China .

articles.title: Bangladesh's ex-PM Sheikh Hasina says she plans to return on 16 December
articles.summary: Hasina has spoken several times of her desire to return, but this is the first time she has set a date.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Sheikh Hasina has been living in exile in India since 2024 By Zoya Mateen BBC News ,  Reporting from Delhi 
- Published 24 November 2026 
Bangladesh's former prime minister Sheikh Hasina has said she plans to return home on 16 December, more than two years after a popular uprising forced her from power. 
Hasina, who has lived in exile in Delhi since August 2024, has asked the Bangladeshi government to fly her back to Dhaka, her spokesperson said. 
The announcement comes amid renewed unrest in Bangladesh, where supporters of her Awami League party have staged protests despite a ban on its activities. 
But it's unclear how Hasina will return. Last year, a Bangladeshi court sentenced her to death in absentia for crimes against humanity over a deadly crackdown on student-led protests that ended her 15-year rule . She denies the charges. 
Bangladesh's state minister for foreign affairs Humayun Kabir dismissed the prospect of Hasina returning on her own terms. 
"Sheikh Hasina will not be able to return to the country as an ordinary commercial passenger; she will be brought back in handcuffs," he told a press briefing on Tuesday. 
Kabir also accused Hasina and Delhi of fomenting recent unrest in Bangladesh, alleging that they were backing "terrorist activities" in the country. 
India's foreign ministry did not immediately respond to a ​request for comment. In April, ​the ministry said it was ⁠examining Bangladesh's request to extradite her and that it wanted to "engage constructively with the new government and further strengthen bilateral ties". 
Hasina fled to India on 5 August 2024 as tens of thousands of protesters descended on Dhaka, and crowds stormed her official residence. 
What began as student protests against quotas in government jobs turned into a mass uprising against her government following a deadly crackdown on demonstrators. The UN estimates that up to 1,400 people were killed during the unrest. 
On Tuesday, Hasina's spokesperson Syed Mozammel Ali accused Bangladeshi authorities of forcing her into exile in violation of the country's constitution. 
"Since Sheikh Hasina was flown to India on a Bangladesh aircraft on 5 August 2024, she now calls upon the government to arrange for her air transport from Delhi back to Dhaka," he said in a statement. 
The choice of date is significant. Bangladesh celebrates Victory Day on 16 December, marking the end of its 1971 war of independence from Pakistan. Hasina's father, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, led the country's independence movement. 
Abu Obaidha Arin, an aide to Hasina, described her decision as "deeply symbolic". "We firmly believe that she will celebrate this historic day among her people," he said, expressing confidence that she would once again lead Bangladesh. 
Hasina's announcement - and Dhaka's sharp response to it - come at a time when the ousted leader is seeking to reassert her political relevance from exile. 
The Awami League was banned from political activities in May last year under the interim government led by Nobel Peace Prize laureate Muhammad Yunus, which took charge after Hasina's ouster. 
The party was subsequently barred from contesting February's general election, which brought its long-time rival, the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), to power, with Tarique Rahman becoming prime minister. 
But the ban has not put an end to street protests by Awami League supporters, who have also called for nationwide shutdowns demanding Hasina's return. 
Hasina, meanwhile, has repeatedly spoken of her desire to return to Bangladesh, even as she has acknowledged the risks of doing so. 
"I know that they may put me in jail or they may kill me, anything may happen, but still I have to go back," she told a gathering of journalists in Delhi over an audio link in August, on the second anniversary of her ouster. 
Hasina's continued political activities from Indian soil have also complicated Delhi's efforts to rebuild ties with Dhaka. 
India enjoyed close relations with Hasina during her 15 years in power and had hoped that the election of a new government in Bangladesh would offer an opportunity to reset ties, which deteriorated sharply after her ouster. 
But nine months after taking office, Rahman is yet to visit India despite an invitation. He has travelled to China, Japan and Malaysia, and skipped the BRICS summit hosted by India in September. 
Discussions over a possible visit in August coincided with anger in Dhaka over Hasina's remarks to journalists in Delhi. 
The two countries have since resumed talks about a visit, but no dates have been announced.

articles.title: US to blacklist Asian AI firm Megaspeed after Nvidia scandal
articles.summary: Megaspeed has been accused of funneling AI chips to China after a former executive's affair with Jensen Huang became public.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images By Kali Hays Technology reporter 
- Published 23 November 2026 
The US has said it intends to ban a Singaporean artificial intelligence (AI) company allegedly tied to the Nvidia scandal from doing business in America. 
The Department of Commerce announced it planned to add Megaspeed Ltd to a list of entities that are blacklisted from buying or selling goods in the US. 
The company is mainly a developer of data centres, but in recent weeks a former executive of Megaspeed was accused of working as a spy for China while having a romantic relationship with Nvidia head Jensen Huang. 
The relationship led to additional scrutiny by US officials and heightened concern that Megaspeed was funnelling Nvidia's advanced AI computer chips to China. 
When exactly the ban against Megaspeed will go into effect was not specified in the commerce department announcement. The BBC has asked the agency for comment, along with the White House and Megaspeed. 
Megaspeed was not well known within the US until last month when media reports emerged that a former Megaspeed executive, Alice Huang, had an affair with Jensen Huang. 
Alice Huang (no relation) was thought by US intelligence to be working as an asset for Beijing, creating national security concerns within the US. 
China has denied that she is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" on AI technology. 
On 12 November, Jensen Huang resigned after allegations he had had another affair, this one with a Nvidia employee. 
On Monday, Nvidia's board reinstated him after US President Donald Trump said he had "convinced" the company and "made the deal". 
The commerce department has said it had been investigating Megaspeed for almost two years. 
The department said it had suspected the company was violating US export controls by helping to get Nvidia's chips into the hands of companies within China. 
China has been blocked from buying such technology since 2022. 
Although based in Singapore, Megaspeed has significant business dealings in China. 
Alibaba, for instance, the major Chinese online retailer, has been reported to be one if its largest customers. 
Megaspeed was a known buyer of billions of dollars of Nvidia computer chips, including through its subsidiary Speedmatrix, which has also been added to the Commerce blacklist. 
Nvidia's computer chips, originally designed for use in gaming consols, in recent years have become crucial to the continued growth of the AI industry. 
Without enough supply or access to computer chips that are capable of processing the huge amount of data needed to make things like AI chatbots and models run, AI companies will not be able to meet or grow demand from people using AI tools. 
That has driven up the value of Nvidia on the stock market, as well as its influence in the AI industry and the White House. 
Although tech stocks have in recent months been volatile and trending lower, when Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia because of his affairs, the company's stock fell by more than 30%. 
Anxiety about the company's influence and ability to operate within the AI ecosystem without its famed executive appeared to take down shares of other tech companies, too. 
Huang was reinstated on Monday to his position as head of Nvidia, a move that US President Donald Trump said he told the company's board to take . 
The company's stock rallied on his reinstatement, as did several other tech stocks, but shares of Nvidia did not climb to where the company had been before being immersed in scandal. 
In the weeks ahead, Huang and the company he now runs again are facing multiple government agency investigations. 
Huang and the chief legal officer of Nvidia are set to appear next for a closed-door briefing with the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

articles.title: India pledges $1.6bn to Nepal in reset of ties
articles.summary: As Nepal rebuilds after deadly floods, its prime minister sets contentious issues aside to secure Indian funding, port access and a new train service.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
The two prime ministers exchanged gifts, inspected a military guard of honour and jointly flagged off a new cross-border train service By Azadeh Moshiri South Asia Correspondent ,  Reporting from Delhi 
- Published 23 November 2026 
Nepal's Prime Minister Balen Shah has repeatedly called for his country to be treated as an equal by its powerful neighbours. His first visit to the Indian capital, Delhi, put that approach to the test, as both sides sought to reset a relationship strained by years of friction. 
The contrast between the two leaders was striking. 
Shah, 36, wearing his trademark black suit and sunglasses, stood beside Prime Minister Narendra Modi, 76, dressed in white. Shah rose to power after a wave of Gen Z-led protests toppled his predecessor. 
Modi, meanwhile, is serving a third term and has recently faced student-led protests in India. 
Yet, the two leaders seemed determined to project warmer relations. They exchanged gifts, inspected a military guard of honour and jointly flagged off a new cross-border train service. 
For Nepal, the stakes were about far more than repairing diplomatic ties. 
The two countries announced a series of agreements covering trade, hydropower, transport and education for Nepali youths. 
India, more crucially, unveiled a $1.6bn (£1.22bn) support package as Nepal recovers from devastating floods earlier this year. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
According to Nepal's estimates, the cost of rebuilding the region hit by a devastating flash flood in September could amount to $4.8bn 
The floods killed more than 1,400 people, with thousands still missing. Shah's government has faced criticism over support for families which lost homes and loved ones. 
The country faces a huge reconstruction challenge. The government estimates rebuilding could cost as much as $4.8bn. Addressing the UN General Assembly in September, Shah warned that when climate disasters devastate poorer countries, "the answer cannot simply be another mega-loan". 
Modi pledged nearly $1.6bn in Indian support. Most of it will come as a line of credit for energy projects, alongside about $400m in grants for reconstruction and infrastructure. 
While Nepal would have preferred a larger package, former senior Nepali diplomat Vijay Kant Karna says it is still "a significant amount" and could help stabilise a relationship that has often been uneasy. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Although the joint statement acknowledged outstanding issues, the two leaders did not mention the border dispute in their public remarks 
A Hindu-majority nation wedged between India and China, Nepal has long had to navigate competing interests from its two giant neighbours. Allegations of political interference and an unresolved border dispute have frequently complicated ties with India. 
Nepal's former Prime Minister, KP Sharma Oli, who leads a communist party, was widely viewed as being closer to China. Shah, by contrast, emerged as a political outsider when he was elected earlier this year. The former rapper, then 35, led a party that was only four years old. 
His new approach of dealing with India may explain why the border dispute was largely absent from the leaders' public remarks, although the joint statement acknowledged that outstanding issues remained. 
According to Govind Pokharel, a former vice-chairman of Nepal's National Planning Commission, Shah's government may have chosen to set contentious issues aside in order to secure progress on more immediate development needs. 
"Right now you can go home and convince the young Nepalis that it will be handled later," Pokhrel says, "but if they don't deal with these issues in the future, there will be criticism." 
Veteran Indian diplomat Anil Trigunayat says both sides appear to have opted to leave the dispute to established mechanisms rather than engage in what he calls "cartographic aggressions". 
There were other gains for Nepal as a result of the Delhi visit. 
As a landlocked country heavily dependent on India for trade, Nepal secured access to two additional Indian ports, Kandla and Paradip. The two sides also agreed to improve road and rail connectivity. 
The leaders jointly inaugurated a train service linking Ayodhya in India, revered by Hindus as the birthplace of Lord Ram, with Janakpur in Nepal, traditionally regarded as the birthplace of his wife Sita. 
There was, however, disappointment on aviation. 
Nepal has long sought greater access to Indian airspace in order to attract international traffic to its airports at Bhairahawa and Pokhara. 
Some analysts believe the lack of an agreement reflects Indian concerns over Chinese involvement in the two airport projects. 
"The airport in Pokhara can pose certain security challenges for India, so it is a more complicated issue to resolve," says Trigunayat. 
India did, however, agree to make an existing air route linking Kathmandu, Bhairahawa and Lucknow bidirectional. 
"Nepal invested a huge amount of money in those airports," says Pokharel. "It fell short of expectations, but the bidirectional route is a breakthrough." 
Shah must now manage relations with China as he seeks to balance the interests of Nepal's two much larger neighbours. 
For now he returns home with substantial financial commitments from India as Nepal continues the long task of rebuilding.

articles.title: US attorney general dodges questions about Nvidia investigation
articles.summary: Nvidia's share price have fallen 7% as lawmakers demand answers about President Donald Trump's involvement in Huang's reinstatement.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
How Nvidia is reacting to Jensen Huang's return as CEO By Rachel Clun   and   Michael Race ,  Business reporters 
- Published 24 November 2026 Updated 1 hour ago 
US Attorney General Todd Blanche has backed Nvidia as a "good corporate citizen" while refusing to comment on whether the AI chipmaker was under federal investigation. 
Blanche said he had no information about newly reinstated CEO Jensen Huang's security clearance status, as lawmakers demand answers about President Donald Trump's involvement in Huang's comeback. 
Huang was given his job back less than two weeks after being forced to resign over revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. 
Asked several times on Tuesday if the justice department or FBI had investigated Huang, Blanche responded: "I don't know what you're talking about." 
Huang is still set to appear before Congress next week, where he will be questioned about national security concerns over his relationship with an alleged China spy who led Megaspeed, a Singapore-based corporate customer of Nvidia. 
Trump has said he would consider pardoning Huang for any potential criminal activity, though he does not think it will come to that. 
"It's always an option, I guess, but I don't think it'll be necessary," Trump told the New York Post in an interview published on Tuesday. 
- 
With Huang rescue, Trump riskily ties his political fortunes to Nvidia 
- Published 3 hours ago 
The US commerce department has also announced it was preparing to blacklist the tech company Megaspeed, which has been suspected of helping to divert advanced chips to China. 
In a joint statement last week, the commerce and justice departments said they began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations" . 
But speaking to reporters on Tuesday, Blanche said the latter department has "hundreds, if not more" export investigations occurring at any one time. 
"So when you say the export investigation is still ongoing, I don't know what you're talking about," he said. 
Asked if he was satisfied Nvidia had been co-operative with any efforts to get to the bottom of whether the company or Huang potentially knew about any chips being diverted to China, Blanche said: "I have no reason to stand up here and say Nvidia is anything but a good corporate citizen. 
"Obviously, if Nvidia was the target or was subject to some criminal investigation or they were obstructing or thwarting our investigation, then that wouldn't be the message that the president is saying to the American people. 
"It shouldn't be what my message would be either." 
While Nvidia's stock market value surged on the announcement of Huang's reappointment, some of the gains were reversed in volatile Tuesday trading. 
The company's share price closed down nearly 6% - still well above where it ended last week. On Monday, Nvidia stock rocketed more than 31% following news of Huang's return. 
Huang reportedly apologised to Nvidia employees on Tuesday, the day after returning to the company as chief executive, saying he made "terrible mistakes" and is now in therapy for 90 minutes per day. 
- 
Faisal Islam: Fears over the AI boom haven't gone away 
- Published 10 hours ago 
The company's board reinstated Huang on Monday in a shock U-turn. Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia's board, said Huang's return was in the "best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers". 
The board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk. 
On Monday, Trump said he spoke to the company's directors and convinced them to bring back Huang . 
Huang's reinstatement provoked bipartisan anger. 
Republican congressman Don Bacon said Nvidia should have "ignored the Administration's inexplicable desire to save Huang". 
Republican Senator Pete Ricketts said Huang's behaviour "doesn't absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips". 
Democratic congressman Robert Garcia, the incoming chairman of the House oversight committee, said Trump's "direct involvement" with Nvidia's decision "raises serious national security and corruption questions". 
Democratic Senator Ruben Gallego said Congress needed to "investigate what stock positions took place before the announcement".

articles.title: China-linked network using AI fakes to smear Taiwan election candidates, BBC Verify finds
articles.summary: The network attacked key figures in the ruling DPP, including President Lai and mayoral candidate Shen.
articles.full_text:
By Sam Howarth   and   Matt Murphy ,  BBC Verify 
- Published 5 hours ago 
Taiwan's ruling party is being repeatedly targeted with AI videos spreading false claims about its leader and other key members ahead of crucial local elections, BBC Verify has found. 
A China-linked network has pumped out more than 500 fake videos about the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) in the past year, which experts suggest is part of a long-running campaign to influence the outcome of the elections. 
The videos appear to try to smear President Lai Ching-te by claiming he holds a US green card - and would abandon Taiwan if war broke out with China - which Taiwan's presidential office says is completely false. Deepfakes also appear to show Puma Shen, who is running to be the mayor of capital Taipei, using drugs, which he denies. Others seek to undermine or ridicule the politicians by showing them in children's clothing or as popular film characters. 
The Taipei mayoralty has traditionally served as a springboard to the presidency. Experts say this has made Shen, who has been openly critical of Beijing, an obvious target for disinformation campaigns. The current mayor, Chiang Wan-an, is part of Taiwan's Kuomintang (KMT) party, which favours closer ties with China. 
Taiwan is a self-governing island that China claims as part of its territory. Beijing and Taipei have long observed an uneasy status quo under which Taiwan, backed by the US, neither formally declares independence nor unites with China. 
But tensions have risen since the DPP came to power in 2016. Beijing has repeatedly accused the party of pursuing independence while China's leader Xi Jinping, who has said "reunification" with Taiwan is a key goal, has stepped up pressure against the party with increased military activity around the island. 
Experts believe the current disinformation activity is part of a broader campaign against Taiwan designed to undermine trust in its democratic process. 
Image caption, 
The campaign has targeted Taiwan's President Lai (top) and his predecessor Tsai (bottom) 
"The account operators are trying to make people distrust the DPP politicians so that they will not believe whatever they say," Austin Horng-En Wang, an expert in cognitive warfare at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, told BBC Verify. "If you don't trust that candidate then you will not listen to what they say," he added. 
The videos, many of which were shared from an account called "noxparable" or carried a watermark with the same name, have been viewed tens of millions of times across several social media platforms since May 2025. 
More than half of those views were tracked in the past four months as the activity has ramped up ahead of the elections. Many of the accounts involved in spreading disinformation listed their locations on social media as mainland China and Hong Kong, while a number of the clips carried labels showing they were generated with AI. Many people who engaged with the videos were often seen repeating the false claims or attacking DPP figures in the comments, while others appeared to treat the clips as entertainment. 
One of the most widely shared videos targeted Shen by superimposing his face onto a man who is seen holding a lighter and exhaling smoke alongside claims he is smoking drugs. The video appears to build on accusations from Taiwan's opposition party that he supports drugs decriminalisation, which Shen denies, and was debunked by a local news network. 
Shen has taken legal action against people sharing deepfakes, local media reported, while his campaign office said AI videos showing the candidate appeared to be part of a "classic tactic China uses to smear specific targets". BBC Verify contacted the Chinese embassy in London for comment. 
Image caption, 
Many of the fake videos ridiculed President Lai and Shen while others portrayed other KMT candidates such as Ko Chih-en (above) in a positive light 
Other debunked claims include allegations that Lai's predecessor Tsai Ing-wen had fraudulently obtained her PhD from the London School of Economics. The university pushed back on identical allegations in 2019 and confirmed it had awarded her the doctorate. 
A number of the social media accounts BBC Verify identified as sharing the disinformation videos appeared to be linked to Chinese firm Borderless, which produces websites that blend apolitical content with pro-China messaging. The network has also been investigated by journalists at the Taiwanese independent media outlet The Reporter, who shared their findings with BBC Verify. Borderless has previously been accused of carrying out "cognitive warfare" against Taiwan by Taipei's National Security Bureau and the firm has been contacted for comment. 
Analysts confirmed to BBC Verify there were also linguistic clues that the accounts, which presented themselves as based in Taiwan, were actually posting from China. The posts occasionally used a simplified Chinese script introduced by the Communist government which was never adopted in Taiwan. 
The posts mostly appeared during regular office hours, which Wang suggested showed a "professional" operation, while the accounts originating outside Taiwan showed evidence of election interfering. "When they pretended to be citizens in another country and used these accounts to manipulate the public opinion of the other country during the campaign, it is definitely election interference," Wang added. 
Earlier this month, Taiwan's central election commission aired an advert warning voters to "beware of AI-generated deepfake videos" circulating online that could seek to influence the upcoming election. It comes as government officials flagged nearly 2,700 social media accounts to Meta that it claimed were part of a Chinese information warfare campaign, Reuters reported. Meta said it had removed the accounts. 
Andrew Yeh of the China Strategic Risk Institute said the ultimate goal is not to favour any party. "China's information operations succeed not just by backing one candidate or opposing another, but by diluting Taiwan's policy debates, driving polarisation and degrading Taiwanese citizens' trust in their democratic processes," he said. 
"Regardless of whether the KMT or DPP comes out on top, a more fractured and more divided Taiwan is in Beijing's interests."

articles.title: Nato chief vows defence against space threat after Russian nuclear satellite reports
articles.summary: German media said Russia planned to launch a satellite with a nuclear warhead into space in coming weeks.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Nato chief Mark Rutte and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz respond to reports of Russian plans to launch nuclear weapons into space By Helen Davidson 
- Published 24 November 2026 
Nato chief Mark Rutte has said the alliance will defend against any threats in space after German reports that Russia is preparing to launch a nuclear-armed satellite. 
Intelligence reports about a possible launch in the next 60 days had been shared among Nato countries this month, according to German media. It was not clear which country had authored the reports. 
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said such reports were "not new, yet they remain no less shocking", and a government spokesman said the reports were being taken "very seriously". 
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he had not seen the reports but dismissed stories citing "unknown sources" as "hardly worth taking seriously". 
The Russian embassy in Berlin told German media it rejected what it called "unfounded allegations" and said the reports were part of a "propaganda campaign". 
Citing anonymous German military and intelligence sources, public broadcasters NDR and WDR and newspaper Süddeutscher Zeitung, said the Russian satellite was dubbed "Sputnik-S" and was equipped with a nuclear warhead. It could be used to disrupt or destroy other satellites, including important communication and observation satellites. 
Asked about the reports, the Nato secretary general told a press conference in Berlin alongside Merz: "We will always make sure we defend every inch of Nato territory, and that includes making sure we are safe when it comes to the space element." 
The Western defensive alliance had a variety of response options, said Rutte. 
"When it comes to the military domain, we will always make assessments of our deterrence and defence and make updates where necessary." 
Merz did not confirm or deny the reports of Russia's plans, but said they "reveal the level of escalation Russia is evidently prepared to pursue". 
German government spokesman Stefan Kornelius warned against causing "excessive nervousness regarding hypothetical dangers". 
Josef Aschbacher, the head of the European Space Agency, told the Handeslblatt newspaper that having nuclear weapons in space was "the ultimate nightmare scenario". 
Russia is a signatory to the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which bans weapons of mass destruction from orbit. 
Bleddyn Bowen, co-director of the Space Research Centre at Durham University, said that exploding a nuclear weapon in space would have "massive infrastructural effects" as there were now more than 15,000 active satellites. But he told the BBC's Today programme that "the effect of these weapons would be extremely indiscriminate and also take out a lot of Russia's own space infrastructure". 
Other countries, including the US and China, have deployed or plan to deploy other weapons in space, exploring other capabilities outside of the treaty, such as targeting rivals' satellites - which are key for military communications, surveillance and navigation. 
In 2024 the US accused Russia of developing a "space-based" anti-satellite weapon armed with a nuclear warhead. Russia denied the accusation . 
"Our position is clear and transparent. We have always been categorically against the deployment of nuclear weapons in space and we are still against it," President Vladimir Putin said at the time. 
In September the US Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said the US had "on-orbit, space-control weapons" circling the planet, but did not provide specifics. In response to the announcement, the Kremlin's Peskov told Russian media that space "must be free of any weapon".
